problem.title: Git hosting for a fast-growing engineering organization
problem.context: A software company hosts its own Git service for 3,000 engineers in four regions. Its CI system starts about 40,000 jobs a day, each fetching a repository. The largest repository has 15 years of history and is about 200 GB; most engineers touch only a small part of it. The service runs in the company's cloud account, and a team of five engineers builds and operates it.

requirements.text: Accept pushes and serve fetches and clones for every repository over the standard Git protocol.
Let engineers work on the largest repository without downloading all of it.
When any single machine or disk is lost, no pushed commit is lost.
When one server fails during working hours, pushes and fetches continue within one minute, without an operator.
A CI job in any region fetches the latest state of a repository within 30 seconds at the 95th percentile, even right after a push.
A fetch that starts after a push has succeeded always sees that push.
Five engineers build and run the service.
Engineers keep using standard Git clients; no custom client may be required.

values: Repository storage: Replicated immutable Git objects in cloud object storage
Serving topology: Stateless Git protocol gateways across regions
Consistency: Quorum-committed push metadata with authoritative post-push reads
Large repository access: Standard Git partial clone with blob filtering
points.description: Replicated immutable Git objects are stored in cloud object storage, while stateless gateways in multiple regions serve Git clients. Pushes become visible after quorum-committed metadata updates, and authoritative post-push reads ensure clients observe the committed state; partial clone blob filtering limits large-repository transfers. Trade-off: This provides durable, horizontally scalable, multi-region access and efficient large-repository checkout, but pays replication and quorum latency/costs and depends on object-storage availability. Partial clones also shift some cost and complexity to later blob retrieval.

values: Repository storage: Synchronously replicated block storage across three zones
Serving topology: Active-passive Git servers with automatic leader failover
Consistency: Single-writer repository metadata with synchronous replication
Large repository access: Standard Git partial clone with blob filtering
points.description: The system stores repositories on block storage synchronously replicated across three zones, with one active Git server serving writes and a passive server ready to assume leadership. Repository metadata remains single-writer and synchronously replicated, while clients use partial clone blob filtering for large repositories. Trade-off: This provides strong metadata consistency, zone-level durability, automatic failover, and reduced large-clone transfer. It gives up write latency and operational simplicity due to synchronous cross-zone replication, keeps standby capacity underused, and makes clients depend on fetching omitted blobs when needed.

values: Repository storage: Eventually replicated object storage with regional caches
Serving topology: Regional read replicas with a central push endpoint
Consistency: Asynchronous metadata propagation between regions
Large repository access: Standard Git partial clone with blob filtering
points.description: Repositories are stored in eventually replicated object storage, with regional caches serving regional read replicas while pushes go through a central endpoint. Metadata propagates asynchronously between regions, and clients use Git partial clone with blob filtering to fetch only needed large-repository content. Trade-off: This improves regional read performance, storage scalability, and large-repository transfer efficiency. It gives up immediate cross-region metadata freshness and local write latency, while central pushes remain a potential bottleneck and cached or replica data may temporarily lag.

values: Repository storage: Replicated immutable Git objects in cloud object storage
Serving topology: Stateless Git protocol gateways across regions with commit-aware caches
Consistency: Quorum-committed push metadata with cache invalidation before success
Large repository access: Standard Git partial clone with blob filtering
points.description: Git objects are replicated immutably in cloud object storage, while stateless regional gateways serve Git traffic through commit-aware caches. A push succeeds only after metadata reaches quorum and affected caches are invalidated; clients can use partial clone to fetch only required blobs. Trade-off: This provides durable storage, regional scalability, and fresher read results, but quorum coordination and invalidation increase push latency and operational complexity. Partial clone reduces initial transfer costs but can add on-demand fetch latency and depends on client support.

values: Repository storage: Synchronously replicated block storage across three zones
Serving topology: Stateless Git protocol gateways across regions
Consistency: Single-writer repository metadata with synchronous replication
Large repository access: Standard Git partial clone with blob filtering
points.description: Repositories reside on block storage synchronously replicated across three zones, while a single authoritative metadata writer replicates its updates synchronously. Stateless Git gateways in each region serve clients and route operations to that writer and storage, with partial-clone filtering limiting large-repository data transfer. Trade-off: This provides durable multi-zone storage, horizontally scalable regional serving, and reduced clone bandwidth, but synchronous writes and single-writer coordination add latency and make writer or quorum availability a bottleneck; partial clone still requires fetching requested blobs.

values: Repository storage: Replicated immutable Git objects in cloud object storage
Serving topology: Regional read replicas and a designated push leader
Consistency: Leader-committed metadata with fencing and read barriers
Large repository access: Standard Git partial clone with blob filtering
points.description: The system stores immutable Git objects in replicated cloud object storage, with a designated leader accepting pushes and regional replicas serving reads. The leader commits metadata under fencing, while read barriers ensure replicas expose committed state; partial-clone clients fetch only the blobs they request. Trade-off: This gains durable storage, scalable regional reads, and consistent ref visibility, but gives up local write availability and adds replication, fencing, and barrier complexity. Partial clones reduce initial transfer and local storage while making some operations depend on later blob fetches.

values: Repository storage: Replicated immutable Git objects in cloud object storage
Serving topology: Stateless Git protocol gateways across regions with commit-aware caches
Consistency: Quorum-committed push metadata with cache invalidation before success
Large repository access: Standard Git partial clone with blob filtering and sparse checkout
points.description: Replicated immutable Git objects in cloud object storage are served through stateless, cross-region protocol gateways using commit-aware caches. Pushes succeed only after metadata is quorum-committed and relevant caches are invalidated, while clients can use Git partial clone and sparse checkout to avoid downloading unnecessary blobs. Trade-off: This gains durable replication, scalable regional serving, and reduced large-repository transfer costs. It gives up some push latency and operational simplicity because quorum commits and coordinated cache invalidation are required; partial clones also make access dependent on later blob retrieval.

values: Repository storage: Synchronously replicated block storage across three zones
Serving topology: Stateless Git protocol gateways across regions
Consistency: Single-writer repository metadata with synchronous replication
Large repository access: Standard Git partial clone with blob filtering and sparse checkout
points.description: Three-zone synchronous block storage provides durable repository data, while a single writer serializes metadata updates and synchronously replicates them. Stateless gateways in each region serve Git clients and use partial clone, blob filtering, and sparse checkout to limit large-repository transfer. Trade-off: This gains strong durability, metadata consistency, and regional serving with reduced large-repository bandwidth, but synchronous replication and the single writer add write latency and can constrain write availability or throughput. Partial clone also shifts some complexity to clients and later object retrieval.

values: Repository storage: Replicated immutable Git objects in cloud object storage
Serving topology: Stateless Git protocol gateways across regions
Consistency: Leader-committed metadata with fencing and read barriers
Large repository access: Standard Git partial clone with server-side sparse filtering
points.description: Stateless Git protocol gateways in each region serve clients, reading replicated immutable Git objects from cloud object storage. A leader commits metadata, while fencing and read barriers ensure gateways observe authorized, ordered state; standard partial clone with server-side sparse filtering limits large-repository transfers. Trade-off: This provides regional horizontal scalability, durable object replication, and consistent metadata while reducing bandwidth for partial consumers. It gives up simpler serving and some availability or latency during leader coordination, and object-storage access plus filtering add operational complexity.

What if asynchronous regional replicas and caches optimize local reads?

adrs.title: Choose durable repository object storage
adrs.context: A single machine or disk loss must not lose a pushed commit, and five engineers must operate the platform. Managed replicated object storage limits storage operations; synchronous multi-zone block storage offers a direct durability model but introduces a tightly coordinated write path.

options.name: Replicated cloud object storage
values: Repository storage: Replicated immutable Git objects in cloud object storage
pros: Replicated immutable objects tolerate individual machine or disk loss.
Managed storage reduces custom storage operations.
cons: The service depends on object-storage availability and replication behavior.
options.reason: It supports durability while reducing storage maintenance for the small team.

options.name: Synchronous three-zone block storage
values: Repository storage: Synchronously replicated block storage across three zones
pros: Synchronous zone replication protects persisted data.
cons: Synchronous writes and recovery coordination add latency and operations work.
options.reason: This option favors a direct replicated volume model and is retained as a distinct durability trade-off.

adrs.title: Serve standard Git traffic and recover from a server failure
adrs.context: The service must use standard Git protocol and clients, continue after a server failure within one minute, and serve CI quickly in four regions. Stateless regional gateways offer replaceable serving capacity; regional read replicas improve locality but depend on leader and replica coordination.

options.name: Commit-aware stateless gateways
values: Serving topology: Stateless Git protocol gateways across regions with commit-aware caches
pros: Regional stateless endpoints support standard Git traffic and automated failover.
Commit-aware caches can serve recent refs near CI.
cons: Cache management adds coordination, and latency targets need load evidence.
options.reason: This pairs regional serving with pre-success invalidation for freshness.

options.name: Stateless gateways with a synchronous writer
values: Serving topology: Stateless Git protocol gateways across regions
pros: Regional gateways distribute Git reads and remain replaceable.
cons: The writer remains a common dependency and can constrain throughput.
options.reason: This keeps Git serving stateless while retaining a synchronous central writer.

options.name: Regional read replicas with push leader
values: Serving topology: Regional read replicas and a designated push leader
pros: Local replicas can serve regional fetches.
cons: Replica lag, leader failover, and barriers need operational handling.
options.reason: This prioritizes local reads while using leader coordination to preserve commit order.

adrs.title: Make pushes visible and keep large repositories usable
adrs.context: The largest repository is about 200 GB, so engineers need selective access through standard Git clients. A fetch after a successful push must see that push. Quorum commits with invalidation and leader commits with read barriers can preserve visibility, while partial clone reduces initial transfers but deferred object reads may affect latency.

cons: Quorum coordination and invalidation can add push latency; deferred blobs can affect fetch time.
options.reason: This directly addresses post-push visibility and large-repository access.
